title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Fragment 102 (N. Fuss, from Euler's Adversaria I, pp. 345-346). Fig. 65 shows four arbitrary coplanar points A, B, C, D with a=AB, b=BC, c=CD, d=AD and diagonals p=AC, q=BD. Euler wants the single polynomial relation among the six mutual distances.

The angle y=∠BAC comes from triangle ABC and x=∠CAD from triangle ACD. Their sum x+y=∠BAD comes from triangle ABD. By the law of cosines, cos y=α=(a²+p²−b²)/(2ap), cos x=β=(d²+p²−c²)/(2dp) and cos(x+y)=γ=(a²+d²−q²)/(2ad).

The half-angle formulas and the addition theorem give two expressions:
- sin((x+y)/2)=½√((1−β)(1+α))+½√((1−α)(1+β));
- cos((x+y)/2)=½√((1+α)(1+β))−½√((1−α)(1−β)).
Comparing these with √((1∓γ)/2) and squaring the first gives √((1−α²)(1−β²))=αβ−γ. Squaring again gives 1−α²−β²−γ²+2αβγ=0. In modern terms this says the Gram determinant of three coplanar unit vectors vanishes.

Substituting the cosines and multiplying by 4a²d²p² gives the symmetric relation. Opposite pairs are (a,c), (b,d), (p,q):
Σ_pairs [u²v²(u²+v²) − u²v²(sum of the other four squares)] + Σ_triangles (product of the three squared sides) = 0.
This is the vanishing of the Cayley–Menger determinant of four coplanar points, i.e. the zero-volume case of the tetrahedron-volume formula.

Euler then gives a 'much shorter' derivation. Put z=x+y; then sin x sin y=cos x cos y−cos z. Squaring and using sin²x sin²y=(1−cos²x)(1−cos²y) gives the same identity directly. With X=d²+p²−c², Y=a²+p²−b², Z=a²+d²−q² it becomes 4a²d²p²−a²X²−d²Y²−p²Z²+XYZ=0. This is exactly the right side of the classical edge formula for 144V² of a tetrahedron (three edges a, d, p from one vertex), set equal to zero.

Finally (Fig. 66) Euler takes a point P in a triangle with sides a, b, c and distances x=PA, y=PB, z=PC, where a is opposite A. He rewrites the relation and rearranges it as a quadratic form in x², y², z²:
a²x⁴+b²y⁴+c²z⁴ − x²y²(a²+b²−c²) − x²z²(a²+c²−b²) − y²z²(b²+c²−a²) − a²x²(b²+c²−a²) − b²y²(a²+c²−b²) − c²z²(a²+b²−c²) + a²b²c² = 0.
This is the classical relation between the distances of a point to the vertices of a triangle.
errors: No mathematical errors found. Every expansion was checked: the half-angle and addition step, both squarings, the 4-point polynomial, and the term-by-term regrouping of the triangle-point relation.

Minor gaps: (1) the derivation tacitly assumes C lies inside angle BAD, so that ∠BAD=x+y; the final squared identity removes this restriction, since it also holds for x−y. (2) The phrase 'in triangulo puncto quocunque' is narrower than needed; the relation holds for any point of the plane.

ideas.what: Relation among the six distances of four coplanar points, derived via the angle identity 1−α²−β²−γ²+2αβγ=0
ideas.modern_name: Vanishing of the Cayley–Menger determinant for 4 coplanar points (Euler's four-point relation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (as a corollary of his tetrahedron-volume formula); also Lagrange (1773), Carnot (1806), Cayley (1841, determinant form)
ideas.where_published: Euler's tetrahedron-volume-in-edges formula is in his work on polyhedra (Novi Comm. Petrop., 1750s); the planar relation is its zero-volume case. The exact E-number is not re-verified here.

ideas.modern_name: Euler/Tartaglia-type edge formula for 144V² of a tetrahedron, with V=0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (tetrahedron volume); antecedents in Tartaglia and Piero della Francesca
ideas.where_published: Euler's tetrahedron volume formula (1750s Petersburg memoirs)

ideas.what: Relation between the distances from a point to the three vertices of a triangle
ideas.modern_name: Point–triangle distance relation (specialised Cayley–Menger; for an equilateral triangle a⁴+x⁴+y⁴+z⁴=x²y²+…)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical; often attributed to Euler/Lagrange; determinant form to Cayley
ideas.where_published: Widely known; also printed here in Opera postuma (1862)

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, elegant, but well-known material. It is the planar Cayley–Menger relation and the zero-volume case of Euler's own published tetrahedron-volume formula, printed in Opera postuma since 1862. The Gram-determinant derivation is natural, and nothing here appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. Minor point: in the image the triangle-point labelling is pairs (a,x), (b,y), (c,z), with a=BC opposite vertex A; the transcription preserves this correctly.
